argument:
The Hellenistic Age was a hard time to be Greek. The old city-states had lost their independence, Alexander's empire had fractured, and philosophy turned from politics toward the question of how a person survives circumstances they cannot control. Zeno of Citium, born in 334 BC, thirteen years after Plato died, arrived at that question by accident. He was a merchant. Around 311 BC his ship went down, he swam ashore, and he walked into Athens with nothing. An oracle had once told him to "take on the complexion of the dead." After the wreck, he seems to have decided he knew what that meant.

Stephen West tells the bookstore story: Zeno reading Xenophon on Socrates, asking the shopkeeper where a man like that could be found, and the shopkeeper pointing out the window at Crates the Cynic hobbling past. Cynicism was one branch of the Socratic inheritance, founded by Antisthenes and made famous by Diogenes of Sinope, who lived in a tub, barked at people, carried a lantern at noon looking for an honest man, and told Alexander the Great to stop blocking his sunlight. The word meant dog-like. Cynics held that virtue alone is enough for a good life, and that virtue means living in agreement with nature. Zeno kept both ideas. What he could not keep was the Cynic indifference to physics. When Crates smashed the pot of lentil soup Zeno was hiding under his robe and shouted after him, "Why run away, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has befallen you," Zeno learned the lesson and also learned its limits.

His objection was practical. Stoic tranquility rests on accepting fate, and you cannot rest on fate without an account of why it exists. So Zeno went to the Academy, absorbed the Timaeus idea that everything works out for the best, and built a physics. Only bodies exist, since only bodies can act or be acted upon. Things like love, justice and time are real parts of nature without existing, figments of the mind. Nature is God, and God is the universe: a material whole animated by the divine logos, split into passive elements, earth and water, and active ones, fire and air, mixed as pneuma. The cosmos burns down and reassembles forever, always the same perfect way. Hence fate.

That closes the circle. Human reason is a spark of the logos, so reasoning well is living in agreement with nature, which is virtue, which is happiness, and the freedom from suffering the Stoics called apatheia. West illustrates it with John Locke on Lost telling a withdrawing Charlie that choosing on something other than instinct is all that separates him from the pig in the net. Logic mattered for the same reason: to study argument was to study the logos. Zeno demonstrated it with one hand, open for perception, curled for assent, clenched for comprehension, gripped by the other hand for knowledge.

Cleanthes organized these ideas in his "Hymn to Zeus." Chrysippus, credited with over seven hundred books, made Stoic logic serious enough to be argued against Aristotle's. None of their complete works survive, only fragments and later, often hostile, commentary. What survives instead is what the late Stoa did with the ethics, and West leaves the listener there, with Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius waiting in the next episode.
keyIdeas: The stoics pictured logic, physics, and ethics as an egg's shell, yolk, and white: distinct but interdependent, so ethics can't be properly understood without the physics and logic that ground it.

Stoicism evolved directly out of cynicism (Zeno studied under the cynic Crates), keeping the cynic emphasis on virtue and living according to nature but adding the physics and metaphysics cynicism lacked.

The stoic universe is pantheistic: God is not a being outside the universe but the material universe itself, divided into passive nature (raw matter) and active nature (the divine logos/reason that shapes it).

Because reason has had infinite tries at creating and destroying the universe in an eternal cycle and always does it the one perfect way, everything that happens is fated, and accepting that fate rationally is the path to tranquility.

Zeno's hand-gesture demonstration (open palm, closing fingers, closed fist, fist gripped by the other hand) visualized perception, assent, comprehension, and knowledge as increasing degrees of epistemic certainty.
